evals.prompt: write me a python script that merges 3 revenue csv files (rev_apr.csv, rev_may.csv, rev_jun.csv, same columns: date, sku, quantity, unit_price) into one q2_report.csv with an added line_total column, sorted by date
evals.expected_output: Complete script; makes small decisions itself (encoding, date format) and notes them instead of asking; writes a self-check with sample data, runs it, and LEAVES IT IN PLACE so the user can re-run it; report cites actual output.
expectations: A complete, runnable Python script is produced that reads the three input CSV files, writes q2_report.csv, and adds a line_total column computed from quantity and unit_price.
The rows are sorted by parsed dates rather than by raw string comparison, and the transcript shows a produced q2_report.csv whose rows are in date order.

A check that verifies the output (an assert, a test file, or a fixture-building block that asserts on results) was actually executed during the run, with its output visible in the transcript — not merely described.
That check is still present in the output files after the run, so the user can re-run it; a check that was created, executed, then deleted fails this.
Small decisions the user did not specify (such as date parsing, file encoding, or tie-breaking within a date) are stated as choices made, not raised as blocking questions back to the user.

evals.prompt: the stock calculation function in inventory.py is off whenever there's a return order, fix it for me
evals.expected_output: Reads the file before editing; writes a check with a return order and runs it against the ORIGINAL code to see it fail; minimal targeted fix, no drive-by refactoring; reruns the same check to see it pass, and reports actual before/after values.
expectations: The transcript shows inventory.py was read before any edit to it was made.
A check containing at least one return order is written and shown failing against the original code, then shown passing after the fix.
The edit changes only how return orders are applied in calculate_stock; total_units_sold and format_stock_line are left unmodified.
The final report states the before/after evidence (what failed, what now passes, with the actual values) instead of only asserting that the bug is fixed.

evals.prompt: why is the orders API so slow lately, sometimes 5-6 seconds
evals.expected_output: Recognizes this as a problem description, not a fix request: reads orders_api.py, identifies the real causes in it (per-order and per-item queries in a loop, a synchronous external shipping call with retries inside the same loop), cites what it observed, then STOPS — does not modify the file even though the fix is obvious.
expectations: orders_api.py is byte-identical to the original after the run and no fix was applied to it, even though the fix is obvious and the file is sitting right there. Read-only diagnostics the run added to gather evidence (a probe script, a timing harness) do not fail this — editing the subject code, or 'helpfully' fixing it, does.

The assessment identifies at least one of the two real causes seeded in orders_api.py: the N+1 query pattern (a per-order items query and a per-item product query inside the loop) and/or the synchronous per-order call to the shipping API with up to three retries and sleeps inside the listing loop.
Each named cause is either tied to the specific function or lines observed in orders_api.py (or other evidence gathered during the run), or explicitly labelled as an unverified hypothesis.
The response does not end with a promise of pending work; any next steps are offered as options for the user to choose from.

evals.prompt: here are the 12 service files behind our storefront (auth.py, payments.py, search.py, uploads.py, cache.py, emails.py, reports.py, webhooks.py, sessions.py, inventory_sync.py, pricing.py, cleanup.py) — do a quick risk review of each one: what it does and the riskiest thing in it
evals.expected_output: Makes a deliberate fan-out call (delegates per-file work to parallel subagents, or says why direct reading beats delegation at this size); final report has one assessment per file naming the seeded risk, tied to the specific function; conclusions rather than pasted file contents; no blocking questions.
expectations: The final report contains an individual assessment for every one of the 12 service files — none skipped, none merged into a vague group verdict.

For at least 9 of the 12 files, the riskiest issue named matches the seeded flaw: auth.py a hardcoded admin token in source; payments.py the charge exception swallowed so failed charges still mark the order paid; search.py SQL built by string interpolation of user input; uploads.py the user-controlled filename joined into the save path (path traversal); cache.py an unbounded module-level cache that never evicts; emails.py an unbounded retry loop that never gives up; reports.py the entire month of rows loaded into memory for export; webhooks.py payloads trusted without any signature verification; sessions.py session tokens generated with the non-cryptographic random module; inventory_sync.py an unlocked read-modify-write of the stock count under concurrent callers; pricing.py float arithmetic on money amounts; cleanup.py a deletion root that falls back to '/' when the environment variable is unset.

The fan-out decision is made deliberately rather than by default: either the per-file work is delegated to parallel subagents (concurrent agent/task tool calls in the transcript, grouping several files per subagent is fine), or the run states why reading directly is the better call here (e.g. the files are small enough that delegation costs more than it saves). Reading all 12 serially with no such reasoning fails.
Each flagged risk is tied to the specific function or line where it occurs, and the report presents conclusions rather than pasting file contents.
